flags.name: Flag 1 - CF Nav
flags.description: Go to the Cloudflare console and click Manage Account from the options on the left-hand navigation. Select Configurations from the dropdown, then click Lists from the nav bar at the top of the page. A playbook adds a malicious IP to a reusable ____ that WAF and Gateway rules can reference. The flag is what malicious IPs can be added to in this specific context.

hints.description: Look for the reusable object type under <s1-label>Lists</s1-label>.

flags.name: Flag 2 - CF Nav
flags.description: In the Cloudflare console, click Domains from the left-hand navigation and select the one-flare.com zone. From that domain's Overview page, open the Security dropdown in the left-hand menu and choose Security Rules. What is the name of a Custom Rule a SOAR playbook could toggle to block an attacker? The flag is the name of the Custom Rule in place that can block an attacker.

hints.description: The flag is in the custom-rules list.
The flag is the only security rule for <s1-value>one-flare.com</s1-value> that has the <s1-value>block</s1-value> action enabled.
The flag is <s1-answer>Mitigate definite bot traffic</s1-answer>.

flags.name: Flag 3 - Analytics
flags.description: Open Cloudflare's documentation on the WAF attack score at https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/about/waf-attack-score/ and read how the numeric scale is calculated and what the range represents. A request is scored 3 out of 99 by the WAF attack score. What does that tell you? The flag is the finding based on a score of 3.

hints.description: The scale is counter-intuitive — most people guess it backwards.
1 means the WAF is most confident it IS an attack; 99 means clean.
The flag is <s1-answer>Almost certainly an attack</s1-answer>.

flags.name: Flag 4 - Analytics
flags.description: In the Cloudflare console, click Analytics from the left-hand navigation and select HTTP Traffic from the dropdown at the top of the page. Scroll down to the Referers panel. Change the Absolute time range to see data from the last 30 days. In the context of web traffic monitoring, a Referer is the webpage that linked to the resource being requested. In other words, it is inbound traffic from a link. So if a visitor to example.com clicks a link to your site there, the request will include a Referer header saying they came via example.com. The flag is the most prevalentReferer.

hints.description: The flag is under the <s1-label>Requests by volume source</s1-label> section of the page, under <s1-label>Referers</s1-label>.
The store front is 'shop'; the employee portal is 'portal'; the REST gateway is 'api'.

flags.name: Flag 5 - Soledrop
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Open a new browser tab and navigate to <s1-value>https://shop.soledrop.co/status</s1-value> to view the store's public status page.</s1-nav>

The store is publishing an active incident. What is the operation called?
 
<s1-flag example="50">The flag is the name of the operation <s1-value>shop.soledrop.co</s1-value> is under attack by.</s1-value></s1-flag>

hints.description: The banner names the operation currently hitting the store.
Two words after the hyphenated day name — it is a swarm of something automated.

flags.name: Flag 6 - Bot score
flags.description: Open Cloudflare's bot score documentation at http://developers.cloudflare.com/bots/concepts/bot-score/ and read the Bot Groupings subsection to see how score ranges map to bot-likelihood bands. Cloudflare uses Bot Scores to measure the likelihood that an incoming web request is operated by an automated bot rather than a human. A bot score of 1 indicates the highest probability of bot activity, while a bot score of 99 indicates human activity. The flag is the band a bot score of 24 would fall into.

hints.description: Scores 30-99 are in the likely human band. The flag is the band covering scores 2-29.

flags.name: Flag 7 - Logpush
flags.description: Open Cloudflare's Logpush documentation at https://developers.cloudflare.com/logs/logpush/ and review the list of available datasets Logpush can export. Logpush allows Cloudflare to send large volumes of specified traffic logs to storage services, log management providers and SIEMs like SentinelOne. Which dataset carries WAF block and challenge decisions, separately from the HTTP request log? The flag is the name of the dataset.

hints.description: HTTP request logs record every request. Security decisions are a different dataset.

flags.name: Flag 8 - Default time
flags.description: In the SentinelOne console, navigate over to Event Search. The lookback window is the period of time Event Search will look back on and show logs for. A time of 24 hours means that Event Search will show you results for anything matching your query, but only from within the past 24 hours. The flag is the default time range for Event Search.

flags.name: Flag 9 - Data ingest
flags.description:
<s1-nav>In the SentinelOne console, navigate over to Event Search. Make sure the query is empty and the range is set to the last 72 hours. Type dataSource.vendor into the fields search bar and select Cloudflare.</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
With Logpush enabled, Cloudflare can send all the relevant logs to the SentinelOne console for triage and response. Logpush can be configured to handle all sorts of volumes to fit the specific needs of your SOC team.
</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="10,000">The flag is the approximate number of logs coming from Cloudflare.</s1-flag>

flags.name: Flag 10 - Detection
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Navigate over to Detections. Find the detection associated with Credential stuffing</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
Detections are a feature of SentinelOne that allow you to create queries that are applied to all incoming traffic. If a log or set of logs match the pattern they are aggregated into an alert for the SOC team to analyze.

Find the detection associated with Credential Stuffing.
</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="Single Event">The flag is the Rule Type associated with this detection.</s1-flag>

flags.name: Flag 11 - Detection
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Navigate over to Detections. Find the detection associated with Credential stuffing. Click on the Event Search button inside the detection window.</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
When you use Event Search while inside a detection, the Event Search query is automatically populated with the query the detection was using. This allows analysts to save time and find the exact logs and events they are looking for.
</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="">The flag is how many failed login attempts have occurred for the most recent event.</s1-flag>

hints.description: Make sure the lookback window is set to 72 hours and the Detection name is "CF-Access-CredStuffing — Login Brute Force / Credential Stuffing on portal.soledrop.co". The flag is under the failed_logins column.

flags.name: Flag 12 - Detection
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Navigate over to Detections. Find the detection associated with WAF Traversal.</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
Under the 'raised alerts' column, you can see how many alerts a detection rule has raised since being activated.
</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="">The flag is the number of alerts that have been raised by the CF-WAF-Traversal detection rule.</s1-flag>

flags.name: Flag 13 - CF Filtering
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Navigate to Traffic policies from the left menu. Go to the Traffic settings page from the dropdown. Scroll down to Traffic logging.</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
Cloudflare allows users to configure what events actually get logged. 

What is the default scope that Gateway uses when capturing events?
</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="">The flag is the default scope</s1-flag>

flags.name: Flag 14 - Event Search Evidence
flags.description:
<s1-nav>Navigate to Event Search. Clear the search and set the search window to 72 hours.</s1-nav>
<s1-flag-body>
Paste this DNS Tunneling search query into the event search.

<s1-value>class_uid=4003 dataSource.cloudflare_dataset='Gateway DNS' unmapped.QueryName=*
| let fqdn        = lower(unmapped.QueryName)
| let label       = replace(fqdn, '\\..*', '')
| let zone        = replace(fqdn, '^.*\\.([^.]+\\.[^.]+\\.[^.]+)$', '$1')
| let label_len   = len(label)
| let digit_cnt   = len(replace(label, '[^0-9]', ''))
| let digit_ratio = label_len > 0 ? digit_cnt / label_len : 0
| let is_txt      = query.type in:anycase ('txt')
| let src_ip      = src_endpoint.ip
| let host        = device.name
| group
    total_queries = count(),
    uniq_labels   = estimate_distinct(label),
    max_label_len = max(label_len),
    long_labels   = count(label_len >= 40),
    txt_long      = count(is_txt AND label_len >= 20),
    hi_entropy    = count(label_len >= 12 AND digit_ratio >= 0.15),
    device_uid    = any(device.uid),
    evidence      = max_by(unmapped.QueryName, label_len),
    first_seen    = oldest(timestamp),
    last_seen     = newest(timestamp)
  by src_ip, host, zone
| filter (hi_entropy >= 10 AND uniq_labels >= 10) OR (long_labels >= 5 AND uniq_labels >= 5) OR txt_long >= 3
| let reason = txt_long >= 3 ? 'Data-in-DNS exfil (TXT long labels)' : ((long_labels >= 5 AND uniq_labels >= 5) ? 'Long-label DNS tunneling' : 'DGA / high-entropy beaconing')
| let detection_time = simpledateformat(last_seen, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss z', 'America/Chicago')
| sort -uniq_labels
| columns detection_time, src_ip, host, zone, reason, total_queries, uniq_labels, long_labels, txt_long, hi_entropy, max_label_len, evidence, device_uid, first_seen
| limit 100</s1-value>

Detection queries can produce Evidence. Evidence is the key piece of data that caused the detection rule to fire. In this case the evidence is the DNS label, and it is indicative of a tunneling attack.

</s1-flag-body>
<s1-flag example="abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz1234567890c2tunnel.acmecorp-lab.workers.dev">The flag is the string + domain that is cited as evidence. </s1-flag>
